content.thinking:
I need to design the scythe carefully so it reads as a real ~2m weapon, standing upright on a small plinth so it touches the floor per the display convention, with the blade curving to the viewer's right at the top.

I'm figuring out the joint structure -- needing at least a root joint, plus a hinge joint for a hanging charm chain -- and mapping out the shaft's S-curve path through 3D coordinates from the butt spike up through the bend to the top.

Still mapping out shaft and blade coordinates...

Defining the blade outline...

I need to avoid self-intersection near the tip by sampling outer and inner edges separately with slightly offset ranges, keeping the root end flat. I'm also planning to layer the blade with a pale bone-tinted base color before adding further detail layers.

Adding glowing edge extrude...

Now I'm thinking about the bony spine along the outer edge, with a sweep whose radius tapers from thick to thin along the path, giving it an ivory bone look with inward-pointing spikes like ribs or teeth, computed from path points and base directions.

I'm also placing dark cyan fenestration discs as flattened cylinders on both blade faces, and considering a cel-shaded bone material with ink outlines for the final paint treatment.

Thinking about the paint gradient from bone-colored root to cyan steel tip, blending mottled bone tones into steel using nested gradient and cel functions so the shading reads correctly, plus adding mottled scratch textures for wear.

Extruding the outline along Z with front faces lit and back faces in shadow, then adding a second curved back horn in dark purple-bone sweeping behind the main shape, plus extra bone spikes and a ribbed collar/socket ring where the shaft meets the head.

Now I'm working out the exact coordinates where the blade root meets the shaft top, tracing the normal offset to find the inner root point and checking whether the shaft endpoint falls inside or outside the blade's footprint at that junction.

I decide to place the shaft's top endpoint and add a small knuckle sphere straddling the blade for thickness, then shift to designing the shaft's vertebra-like surface detail — sweeping bone-colored ridges along the shaft path with spine plates on one side, computing ridge direction from the tangent at each point.

Still writing vertebra plates...

I'm adding a hanging charm chain of 3-4 linked points below the attachment, using a hinge-style chain with small torus rings and a diamond/lantern shape at the end.

I'm positioning the charm's attach point near the back horn base, offset forward in z to avoid colliding with the blade root, and routing it down to clear the shaft.

Now for the pommel, I'm shaping a bone-lump sphere with a glowing cyan gem in front, then adding crescent-curved claws spreading outward on either side plus a downward spike into the plinth, using curve coordinates to define their sweep and tapering radius.

Next I'm building the ring flare as a glowing torus around the pommel, positioning it with slight tilt, then shaping the butt spike down into the plinth and constructing the plinth itself as a stepped lathe profile to resemble dark bone-stone.

Now I'm adding glowing cyan rune textures as flat planes on top of the plinth, using an SVG texture of circular glyph patterns with transparent background and thick cyan strokes.

Checking the shaft butt placement stays within the plinth bounds, then planning small glowing cyan rune decals along the front of the shaft using decal placement with directional offsets and sizing to mark the surface without disrupting the geometry.

For the magical smoke effect, I'm sketching teardrop-shaped wisp cards with gradient fills in cyan and purple tones, drifting along the blade's inner edge using oriented frames so they lean outward naturally from the surface.

I'm also adding small floating glowing motes near the blade for extra detail, and thinking through how to shape oval fenestrations along the blade spine with a dark inner and cyan glowing rim, working out how to orient a scaled cylinder to get the elongated ellipse shape I want.

Adding a smaller glowing cyan ellipse offset slightly in z to sit as a rim inside the darker eye shape, layering glow beneath and dark on top to avoid z-fighting. I'm also planning bone-colored ridge sweeps along the blade's midline front and back, plus a thicker spine ridge along the outer edge for structural detail.

Now I'm working out backward-angled barb spikes along the outer edge using the normal and tangent vectors to set direction and length, plus inward bone-colored teeth along the inner edge and vertebra-like spikes on the shaft. I'm also planning a spiky radial cluster at the head knot junction in pale tones with dark purple accents.

For the tattered cloth, I'm defining three hanging strips at different attachment points with jagged, irregular outlines built from extruded cross-sections, making sure the outline order stays non-self-intersecting as I trace the jagged edges on each side.

Still refining shaft geometry and texture...

I'm limiting the palette to keep colors under the count budget, then adding leather strap colors and small bronze stud plates along the shaft with glowing cyan rune decals positioned just in front of the plate surfaces.

Writing SVG code...

Adding radial tick marks and a star glyph for the rune circle, then detailing the plinth with bone claws around the rim, a mottled cel-shaded texture, and a thin glowing cyan ring at its base.

Now I'm starting the blade shape implementation, importing the builder, framing, path, paint, and glow utilities I'll need, and double-checking each import actually gets used to avoid lint errors — polyline for ridge sweep points, INK for default outlines.

I'm deciding to skip the inkLines helper on the horns to reduce risk and just rely on INK directly as the hole color, then adding the metadata export with the style and commit info before starting the build function that creates the scythe's root joint.

Now I'm shaping the blade's spine with a curved series of points and defining a width falloff function so it tapers from a thicker base near the root to a sharp point at the tip, simplifying the exponent to keep the curve clean while checking that the inner edge doesn't self-intersect around the midpoint of the spine.

I'm checking the curvature at the tip bend and near the root bend to confirm the blade's width stays smaller than the local radius of curvature, avoiding self-intersection on the concave side, and verifying the tangent calculation returns a vector I can use to compute the normal direction.

Now I'm sketching how to sample the outline: generating outer points along the spine at even intervals, then inner points offset by the width, marking sharp corners at the tip and root, and keeping the total point count low enough for smooth extrusion.

For the blade extrude, I'm configuring thickness, bevel size, and placement so the sharp corners don't get lost from excessive bevel shrinking, then setting up the blade's paint as a gradient between the bone coat and steel coat colors, with a separate glowing cyan strip along the edge.

I'm thinking through the glow strip placement: positioned near the inner edge, offset slightly along the normal so it sits within the blade's thickness and stays hidden on the flat faces, only showing as a bright rim at the edge itself.

Adding fenestration ovals with glowing cyan rims along the blade, scaling their size based on position toward the tip...

Still writing sweep geometry...

Still writing spike geometry...

For wisps, I'm positioning frames along the blade using the tangent and normal vectors, then placing flame cards rooted at the frame with growth directed inward toward the concave side.

Writing wisp SVG path...

Now sketching spirit motes as tiny glowing octahedrons floating near the blade, plus a head knot bone piece with a cyan gem detail on the front.

Working out radial spikes and dark-purple back horns around the knot...

Still spacing vertebra discs and spikes...

For the leather wraps, I'm placing small tori along the shaft at intervals, oriented so their hole axis aligns with the tangent direction, using bone-colored plates for the ridge detail.

Still orienting plates and runes...

Now I'm placing the pommel: an icosahedron bone shape scaled slightly tall, a glowing tilted ring near the top, and a small flattened octahedron gem glowing in front.

For the claws, I'm sweeping tapered curves outward on both sides from mid-blade down to tips, tapering radius to a point with bone coloring, plus smaller hooked secondary claws curving down toward the plinth top.

I'm adding front and back Z-axis claws using mirrored catmull curves tapering to points in dark purple, then placing a butt spike pointing downward from the base into the plinth with dark bone coloring. For the plinth itself I'm lathing a profile outline with flat shading and ten segments.

I define the lathe outline coordinates for the plinth's cross-section, then add six rim claws spaced around the plinth at an angle, each a small cone-shaped spike pointing outward and slightly up, checking that their tips don't collide with the pommel claws above.

Now I'm placing a rune plane just above the plinth top, sized to fit within the rim, oriented flat with its normal pointing up. I'm generating an SVG for the rune circle with concentric rings and tick marks spaced every 30 degrees around the perimeter.

Finishing the SVG with triangular star shapes layered over the ticks, checking the geometry stays within the circle bounds, then moving on to designing hanging tatter shapes attached along the shaft with their own position, yaw, and scale parameters.

Checking the shaft position at that point keeps the hanging tatters clear since they sit slightly ahead in z. For the charm, I'm defining a short chain path hanging straight down from an attach point near the shaft, using a few vertical waypoints for the chain to follow.

I'm adding the ring, connecting rods, and a glowing gem at the chain's end, parenting each piece to the correct joint along the chain. I need to double check that the third joint I'm referencing actually exists in the chain's joint list before using it.

For the floating motes, I'm using flat cyan and purple octahedrons, and I'm noting that parts placed without an explicit bone will auto-attach to whichever joint is nearest — which could accidentally pull something like a head ornament toward the charm joint instead of the head.

So I'm tracing bone segments from root to each charm joint to figure out which segment is closest to the blade tip, since that determines which joint a part near the blade will actually bind to.

To avoid these ambiguous proximity-based bindings entirely, I'm planning to explicitly pass `bone: root` into every part call, defining a shared options object I can spread into sweeps, extrudes, lathes, decals, and cards so nothing accidentally binds to the wrong charm joint.

Still deciding on the charm's swing chain versus skipping the joint entirely, then moving into defining the paint palette with bone-colored mottled tints.

Checking the remaining type usages and imports - confirming unused ones are skipped, gradient/mottle inputs match expected types, and glow/extrude work correctly on sweeps, torus, and decal parts. Now verifying the extrude outline typing and making sure the strip's point arrays are set up properly.

I'm also checking the outline construction to ensure outer and inner points don't cross near the tip, and tracing whether curvature near the root causes the inner edge to fold given the blade's width and turning radius.

Now I'm computing the tooth positions, fenestration widths, and card frame spacing parametrically along the spine to set up the final geometry before writing the complete code.

Still placing the remaining spirit motes with alternating colors, then checking the spike, sweep, and rod helper signatures to confirm I'm passing the right arguments for base, tip, radius, color, and bone. I'm also setting the pommel torus rotation and double-checking the part options structure.
